scope_plain: Every St. Louis County voter (not the City of St. Louis)
office_explainer: Runs St. Louis County government day to day: budget, police, roads, parks and public health.
why_it_matters: First open race for county executive in 52 years; Sam Page is not running. Both major candidates focus on the county budget: Zimmerman pledges to stop using one-time money to plug ongoing gaps, and Hancock opposes new taxes to fix it.

candidates.name: Jake Zimmerman
candidates.background: St. Louis County assessor since 2011; earlier a state representative and an aide to Gov. Bob Holden and Attorney General Jay Nixon. Won the Aug. 4 Democratic primary with 46.5% over state Sens. Brian Williams and Angela Walton Mosley.

own_words.text: "I'm here to get us back to basics and bring real leadership to County government."
"On my watch, there are no backroom deals. On my watch, no special favors for the rich and connected."
Pledges to stop using one-time funds to close structural budget gaps; open to more city-county cooperation if it improves services for county residents (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: Dennis Hancock
candidates.background: County Council member for the 3rd District since 2023; mayor of Fenton for 12 years before that. Won the Republican nomination.

own_words.text: "Fighting out of control crime in and around St. Louis County is my top priority."
"No more kickbacks and no more reckless spending on government projects."
Opposes additional taxes to help with the county government's budget; wants less red tape to boost economic growth (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: J.D. McFarland
candidates.background: Community organizer; previously ran for St. Louis alderman and mayor on the Green Party ticket. Says he has worked for local nonprofits such as Better Family Life and Jobs with Justice.

own_words.text: Describes himself as a "cultural architect" who believes leadership is a responsibility.
Says he wants to build a region that focuses on youth, health and learning (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

scope_plain: Every St. Louis County voter (not the City of St. Louis)
office_explainer: Decides which state crimes get charged in St. Louis County and prosecutes those cases in court.
why_it_matters: Price Smith was appointed in January 2025 after Wesley Bell left for Congress; this is her first race for a full term. Her only opponent is a Libertarian.

candidates.name: Melissa Price Smith
candidates.background: Sworn in Jan. 3, 2025, as the first woman to hold the job; in the prosecutor's office since 2008, where she supervised the Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Team. Former professional ballet dancer. Won the Aug. 4 Democratic primary with 74.1%.

own_words.text: Campaign slogan: "All Prosecutor. No Politics."
Lists priorities including "Combating violent crime" and "Rehabilitating non-violent offenders."
Pledges to continue stricter sentences for gun crimes and more support for people out on bond (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: Theo Brown Sr.
candidates.background: Former police officer in St. Louis and Kinloch and a former St. Louis Community College trustee. Has run for state senator, Riverview Gardens school board and county assessor. No campaign website.

own_words.text: No campaign statements found; St. Louis Public Radio notes he has no campaign website.

scope_plain: Every St. Louis County voter (not the City of St. Louis)
office_explainer: Sets the value of homes, businesses and vehicles, which drives everyone's property tax bill.
why_it_matters: Open seat for the first time since 2011, because Jake Zimmerman is running for county executive. The assessor's values feed into every property tax bill, including the tax measures on this ballot.

candidates.name: Doug Clemens
candidates.background: State representative first elected in 2018; about 30 years in operations management. Says he got into politics over radioactive contamination in north St. Louis County. Won the Aug. 4 Democratic primary with 57.5%.

own_words.text: "Property assessments affect every family, every renter and every small business. They must be handled fairly and transparently."
Pledges an assessor's office focused on customer service (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: David Messner
candidates.background: Developer who has worked in Hermann and on Laclede's Landing; helped relaunch Old Judge Coffee Co.

own_words.text: Says he will work to prevent deed theft and speak up against legislation that could hurt property values (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).
Wants to use the assessor's data to advise policymakers on growth and economic development (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: Austin Brown
candidates.background: Research and development engineer; member of the Young Friends of St. Louis Earth Day.

own_words.text: Says he would be transparent and not give special favors to "big money."
Has pledged no special treatment for data center developments (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

scope_plain: Voters in Missouri's 1st Congressional District: all of the City of St. Louis and much of north and central St. Louis County, including all of Clayton, Rock Hill and part of Webster Groves (2022 map, used again in 2026).
office_explainer: One of Missouri's eight members of the U.S. House. Votes on federal laws, taxes and spending.
why_it_matters: Bell is finishing his first term in a district St. Louis Public Radio calls overwhelmingly Democratic. The 2026 race uses the 2022 lines no matter how statewide Prop A turns out; a yes on Prop A would change the map starting in 2028. The U.S. Supreme Court's Sept. 25 order and the Secretary of State both say the 2022 map is used in November. Nominees were picked in the Aug. 4 primary, which used the 2025 map, so some voters now sit in a different district than in August.
